decision.state: Promising reported employment signal; causal and marginal cost-effectiveness not yet estimable
decision.summary: Farming Hope combines paid culinary apprenticeship, job support, community meals, grocery distribution, and food recovery. Its 2024 report shows high graduation and post-graduation employment rates, but does not publish participant flow, employment definitions, follow-up completeness, a comparison group, or the cost of creating an additional sustained job. Randomized transitional-jobs evidence is mixed and highly program-dependent, so the reported placement rate cannot yet be treated as causal impact.

nativeScale.label: apprentices trained
nativeScale.semantics: organization-reported entrants or participants; the report does not publish an eligible-applicant denominator, duplicate handling, or comparison group

nativeScale.label: employment within 90 days of graduation
nativeScale.semantics: organization-reported rate among an unspecified graduate follow-up denominator; job type, hours, retention, data source, missing follow-up, and counterfactual are not published

nativeScale.label: average wage within one month of exit
nativeScale.semantics: organization-reported average with no published sample size, distribution, job hours, retention, or comparison; it is not an earnings-impact estimate

financialContext.summary: The 2024 Form 990 reports $4.12 million in revenue, $3.30 million in expenses, and $2.83 million in program-service expenses. It assigns $1.71 million of expense to job training, $1.03 million to meals and groceries, and $96,880 to food-waste work.
financialContext.boundary: These are organization-defined annual program buckets, not incremental costs or impact prices. The $1.71 million job-training line includes the full reported program, while the 41-apprentice count lacks the participant-flow and outcome denominator needed for a causal cost per sustained job. Four active city prime-contract records also span meals, groceries, food recovery, and another grant; award authority, payments, and remaining authority are different accounting concepts and none is philanthropic funding room.

evidence.population: 41 apprentices trained in Farming Hope's 2024 culinary employment program
evidence.result: Farming Hope reports an 85% graduation rate, 71% employment within 90 days of graduation, and a $21.29 hourly average wage within one month of exit. It separately reports 149,884 meals cooked and 263,251 pounds of groceries distributed.
evidence.transfer: The report does not identify the employment-rate numerator, missing follow-up, job quality, hours, retention beyond 90 days, pre-program employment, unsuccessful applicants, or a comparison group. Food outputs serve a different objective and cannot be added to employment outcomes or used to infer apprentice impact.

evidence.population: 1,813 men released from prison within the prior 90 days, assigned to transitional jobs or basic job-search assistance
evidence.result: The programs sharply increased employment while subsidized jobs were available, but did not increase regular unsubsidized employment during or after the program; by the end of year two, about one-fifth of each group worked in the formal labor market. Key recidivism measures did not improve.
evidence.transfer: This is strong causal evidence for earlier 30-to-40-hour transitional-jobs models in four Midwestern cities, not Farming Hope's smaller Bay Area culinary apprenticeship. The population, labor market, training content, supports, employer links, and comparison services differ.

evidence.design: Seven-site randomized evaluation and cost analysis
evidence.population: About 7,000 recently incarcerated people or low-income noncustodial parents assigned to enhanced transitional jobs or community services
evidence.result: Across sites, administrative data show final-year employment of 64.4% versus 60.4%, a 4.0 percentage-point impact; four of seven programs improved longer-term employment or earnings. Program costs ranged from about $7,000 to $11,100 per program-group member, and effects varied materially by site and model.
evidence.transfer: The pooled result shows that enhanced models can produce modest longer-term gains, not that every culinary or transitional program does. The study's populations, scale, program components, costs, and local alternatives differ; its per-participant cost is not a benchmark that can be assigned to Farming Hope.

model.nativeOutcome: Apprentice in unsubsidized employment at least 30 hours per week and still employed 12 months after program exit
missingInputs: Eligible applicants, enrolled apprentices, graduates, exits, and all follow-up denominators with missingness
A pre-specified definition of unsubsidized employment, hours, wage, benefits, job quality, and sustained retention
Complete 3-, 6-, 12-, and 24-month employment and earnings follow-up, including unsuccessful exits
A credible Farming Hope comparison or a transparent, sensitivity-tested transfer from external trials
Incremental wages, training, case management, food production, employer-placement, facility, and overhead costs
Separate accounting for apprentice compensation, meal and grocery outputs, earned revenue, and donated food
City-contract reimbursement, public-funding displacement, employer substitution, and philanthropic additionality
Time-bounded $100K, $1M, and $10M capacity plans with cohort size, constraints, and downside cases
model.qalyBoundary: No QALY, WELLBY, life-saved, or life-substantially-bettered conversion is published. Establish incremental sustained employment and earnings, duration, displacement, participant wellbeing, and full marginal cost before selecting and versioning any wellbeing conversion.

reservations: Employment training, community meals, grocery distribution, and food recovery have different beneficiaries, outcomes, evidence, and costs.
The 85% graduation and 71% employment figures do not publish exact numerators, missing follow-up, job definitions, retention, or a comparison group.
The $21.29 hourly average lacks a sample size, distribution, hours, benefits, prior wage, and retention window beyond one month.
Employment during a paid apprenticeship is not the same outcome as sustained unsubsidized employment after exit.
External randomized studies show that transitional-job effects vary by program and may fade after subsidies end.
Form 990 program expenses are organization-wide buckets and cannot be divided by trainees or placements to produce a causal cost per job.
Active public contracts and earned food-service revenue may fund overlapping activities, so the additional activity created by a private gift is unknown.
